extracted.intended_audience: authors and advanced TeX users typesetting mathematical manuscripts (mathematical typesetters / macro writers)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for typesetting long displayed mathematics and for writing/using TeX macros: where to break displays, how to align multi-line equations, macro-definition conventions, debugging and safety practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Author decides display breaks
rubrics_metrics.description: The author of a mathematical manuscript is generally the best judge of how to break long displayed formulas; TeX never attempts to break them because no set of rules is really adequate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Break positions depend on subtle factors of mathematical exposition (e.g., desire to emphasize symmetry or structure); the author should indicate convenient break points rather than rely on an automatic rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inline vs displayed break rule for binary operations/relations
rubrics_metrics.description: Although formulas within a paragraph always break after binary operations and relations, displayed formulas always break before binary operations and relations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: do not end a display line with '+', instead end with the preceding subformula and begin the next line with '+'. This preserves logical grouping and readability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indentation when breaking before binary operation
rubrics_metrics.description: When an equation is broken before a binary operation, the second line should start at least two quads to the right of where the innermost subformula containing that binary operation begins on the first line.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This avoids the binary operator appearing directly under a large left delimiter and makes the continuation visually distinct; use alignment/spacing commands to achieve the offset.

rubrics_metrics.name: Matching delimiters across broken lines
rubrics_metrics.description: You cannot use \left and \right delimiters in isolation across separate lines; the two delimiters must match in size even when they occur in different lines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose the delimiter size yourself (e.g., \biggl and \biggr) and construct the multi-line display so both delimiters are explicit and balanced; use alignment (&) markers to control alignment (they need not be at '=' signs).

rubrics_metrics.name: Two-line (almost flush-left/right) form for long equations
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'two-line' form places the first part almost flush left and the second part almost flush right (where 'almost flush' means one quad away).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is especially recommended for equations with a long left-hand side; typically break just before the '=' sign. Use \displaylines or appropriate alignment macros and sometimes insert an explicit '{}' so TeX treats the following operator as binary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Break at natural phrase / major bracket
rubrics_metrics.description: When a formula is too long for the page width and must be broken into successive lines, it should be broken, if possible, at the end of a natural 'phrase' (for example at the end of one of the major brackets) and not at an inner symbol.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This natural phrasing improves intelligibility between writer and reader; authors should indicate a convenient point of fracture when writing long formulas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid overdisplaying equations
rubrics_metrics.description: Some authors display every equation while others run many equations into text; the tendency to overdisplay is common and can be counterproductive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors may run displayed material into text to shorten and improve papers; conversely, suggest displays where run-in would cause bad line breaks. Use discretion in choosing display vs inline presentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use macros to save typing and ensure consistency
rubrics_metrics.description: Let control sequences stand for constructions that occur frequently; defining macros reduces keystrokes, typographical errors, and inconsistencies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Define macros for clusters of symbols used many times (e.g., a vector notation). Look through the document to identify useful macros; avoid defining a macro solely to save typing for a single isolated formula.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit the number of global definitions in macro files
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not put thousands of definitions into macros.tex because TeX's memory is limited and reading a huge file takes time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A large collection of macro definitions can be a 'format' (e.g., plain TeX format) and should be used judiciously; avoid bloating personal macro files.

rubrics_metrics.name: Macro parameter numbering and ordering
rubrics_metrics.description: In the parameter text of a \def, the first appearance of # must be followed by 1, the next by 2, and so on (up to #9 allowed); parameters must be declared in order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Within the replacement text any of the declared parameters may be used any number of times and in any order; you cannot use #5 unless #4 was previously declared in the parameter text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid unintended spaces in macro definitions
rubrics_metrics.description: Be careful not to put blank spaces before the '{' that begins the replacement text or before parameter markers in the parameter text, because spaces can alter argument scanning behavior.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: \def\row #1 #2 {…} will not behave the same as \def\row#1#2{…} because the spaces tell TeX to look for arguments followed by spaces. Spaces after control words (e.g., after \row when used) are optional as usual.

rubrics_metrics.name: Delimited parameters and argument scanning rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Macros can have parameters that are delimited in quite general ways; a delimited parameter is followed in the parameter text by one or more non-parameter tokens and the corresponding argument is the shortest (possibly empty) sequence of tokens with properly nested braces followed by that delimiter sequence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Undelimited parameters are the next non-blank token (or a braced group if the next token is '{'); when an argument is of the form {nested tokens} the outermost braces are stripped. Category codes and character codes must match when matching delimiters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Braces within arguments affect delimiter matching
rubrics_metrics.description: An argument will not stop when its delimiter occurs inside braces, because that would produce unbalanced braces.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: with \def\cs #1.#2\par{…} the first argument is delimited by a single period; if the invoked text contains a period inside {…}, that period is treated as part of the argument, not as the delimiter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use \tracingmacros to debug macro expansion and argument reading
rubrics_metrics.description: Set \tracingmacros=1 to have TeX write to the log whenever it expands a macro and when it has read a macro argument; this helps understand why a \def behaves unexpectedly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The log will show the macro definition and lines like '#1<-…' giving the actual arguments found, which is invaluable for diagnosing complex macro interactions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guard against runaway arguments with \par rule
rubrics_metrics.description: TeX disallows including \par as part of an argument unless the macro is declared \long; otherwise TeX aborts the expansion and reports a 'runaway argument'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you want a macro to accept paragraph tokens, declare it \long (e.g., \long\def\bold#1{{\bf#1}}), but beware large-argument macros use memory; prefer grouping macros (\begingroup/\endgroup) for multi-paragraph effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use \outer for control sequences that should appear only at quiet times
rubrics_metrics.description: Preceding a definition with \outer makes the control sequence forbidden in places where tokens are being absorbed at high speed (arguments, parameter texts, preambles, conditional text being shipped over).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This helps detect missing-brace or other errors early; for example, define \proclaim as \outer so users don't attempt to state a theorem inside a definition or argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefixes \long, \outer, \global and \gdef semantics
rubrics_metrics.description: A \def may be preceded by \long, \outer, and/or \global in any order; \gdef is equivalent to \global\def.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand the combined effect (e.g., \long\outer\global\def is equivalent to \outer\long\gdef). Use \global when a definition must transcend its group.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use \let to copy a token's current meaning carefully
rubrics_metrics.description: \let\cs=(token) gives \cs the token(s) current meaning; if the token is a control sequence, \cs acquires that significance; if it is a character token, \cs behaves to some extent like that character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware of differences: e.g., after \let\zero=0 you cannot use \zero in a numerical constant because TeX requires actual digit tokens (after macro expansion) for numbers. \let is useful for swapping or temporarily renaming commands.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use \futurelet to peek ahead at the next token
rubrics_metrics.description: \futurelet\a\b sets \a to the token that follows and then expands \b; \b can examine \a and continue processing conditionally based on what comes next.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This technique supports macros that change behavior depending on following tokens; it is a primitive means of lookahead.

rubrics_metrics.name: Put a blank space after numeric constants
rubrics_metrics.description: Always put a blank space after a numeric constant so TeX knows the constant is complete; otherwise TeX may begin expanding following tokens (possibly macros) and this can slow processing or cause subtle errors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The extra space will not appear in the output. Omitting the space forces TeX to read digits until a non-digit is seen and may require backtracking of tokens; for aesthetics authors sometimes omit the space when another character immediately follows to avoid extra spaces in the source.

rubrics_metrics.name: Literal '#' in replacement text is written as '##'
rubrics_metrics.description: To include a single literal # token in replacement text, write '##' in the definition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This common requirement arises when generating code or other macro definitions via macros; exercises illustrate useful examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Brace-delimited parameter special extension (# followed by '{')
rubrics_metrics.description: If the very last character of the parameter text is # so that this # is immediately followed by '{', TeX behaves as if the '{' had been inserted at the right end of both the parameter text and the replacement text, allowing constructs like \def\a#1#{\hbox to #1} so that \a3pt{x} works.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This extension allows defining macros where the size unit is given followed immediately by a braced group argument; be aware of this syntax when designing parameter texts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definitions are local to groups unless made global
rubrics_metrics.description: A control sequence has only one definition at a time; the most recent definition is used, and definitions are local to the group that contains them unless prefixed by \global.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use \global or \gdef if you want a definition to persist beyond the current group; otherwise old definitions will be restored when the group ends.

rubrics_metrics.name: Token matching depends on category and character codes
rubrics_metrics.description: When matching parameter delimiters and tokens, both category codes and character codes must match; control sequence names must be identical.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be careful if you change category codes or use unusual token characters; mismatched category codes will prevent the intended delimiter/argument matching.
